Final Homework - Unsupervised Learning, PCA, and Anomaly Detection¶

Student ID: 313261919
Course: Introduction to Data Science
Dataset: Hugging Face Models Trending
Random seed: 42

Research question¶

What structure exists among currently trending Hugging Face models, and which models look unusual when popularity, age, activity, metadata, and access characteristics are considered together?

This notebook is the report as well as the executable analysis. Explanations, assumptions, mathematical intuition, results, limitations, and ethical reflection appear in Markdown cells next to the relevant code and figures.

Analysis map¶

  1. Dataset selection and feature construction
  2. Exploratory data analysis
  3. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
  4. Sample clustering with K-Means, DBSCAN, and agglomerative clustering
  5. Feature-space clustering
  6. Z-score, Isolation Forest, and Local Outlier Factor anomaly detection
  7. Method comparison, critical reflection, and ethics
  8. Visualization dashboard and reproducibility checks

1. Dataset selection¶

The source is the Hugging Face Models Trending dataset on Kaggle, published by the account zoupet. Its data card states that it is collected daily from the public Hugging Face Hub API to track downloads, likes, releases, task mix, and publisher activity. The official ModelInfo documentation describes the API fields used here; in particular, downloads is the number of downloads over the preceding 30 days, while likes is cumulative.

The frozen CSV contains 156 daily snapshots and 156,000 rows. Reusing all rows as independent observations would over-weight models that appear on many days. The analytical sample is therefore the latest snapshot: 1,000 distinct model repositories, one row per model.

Original fields¶

Field Meaning
snapshot_date Date on which the row was collected
id, author Model repository identifier and publisher
downloads, likes 30-day downloads and cumulative likes
created_at, last_modified Repository creation and latest update timestamps
pipeline_tag, library_name Intended task and associated software library
tags Pipe-separated metadata tags
private, gated Visibility and access controls
license Separate license field in the downloaded file

Why a numerical analysis matrix is constructed¶

The raw file has 13 columns but includes identifiers, dates, and high-cardinality categories. Clustering directly on arbitrary integer codes for those categories would create meaningless distances. I instead construct 13 numerical features with explicit real-world meanings. Counts are log-transformed where their tails are long, then all analytical features are standardized. This gives 1,000 rows and 13 numerical features, satisfying the assignment thresholds while preserving the raw file unchanged.

The sample is real-world and has no anomaly label. gated is an access-control attribute, not an anomaly ground truth.

df = raw.copy()
for column in ["snapshot_date", "created_at", "last_modified"]:
    df[column] = pd.to_datetime(df[column], utc=True, errors="coerce")

latest_date = df["snapshot_date"].max()
models = df.loc[df["snapshot_date"].eq(latest_date)].copy()
assert len(models) == 1_000
assert models["id"].is_unique

models["library_clean"] = models["library_name"].fillna("missing")
models["gated_flag"] = models["gated"].astype(str).str.lower().ne("false").astype(int)
models["tag_count"] = models["tags"].fillna("").str.count(r"\|") + 1
models.loc[models["tags"].fillna("").eq(""), "tag_count"] = 0
models["model_age_days"] = (
    (models["snapshot_date"] - models["created_at"]).dt.total_seconds().div(86_400).clip(lower=0)
)
models["days_since_update"] = (
    (models["snapshot_date"] - models["last_modified"]).dt.total_seconds().div(86_400).clip(lower=0)
)
models["author_model_count"] = models.groupby("author")["id"].transform("size")
models["pipeline_model_count"] = models.groupby("pipeline_tag")["id"].transform("size")
models["library_model_count"] = models.groupby("library_clean")["id"].transform("size")
models["model_id_length"] = models["id"].str.len()
models["library_missing"] = models["library_name"].isna().astype(int)
models["has_license_tag"] = models["tags"].fillna("").str.contains(r"(?:^|\|)license:", regex=True).astype(int)
models["has_arxiv_reference"] = models["tags"].fillna("").str.contains(r"(?:^|\|)arxiv:", regex=True).astype(int)

for source, target in [
    ("downloads", "log_downloads"),

]:

1.1 Analytical feature definitions¶

Feature Interpretation
log_downloads, log_likes Popularity on two different scales; logs prevent a few blockbuster repositories from dominating every Euclidean distance
log_model_age_days Repository age at the snapshot date
log_days_since_update Time since the last recorded update
log_tag_count Metadata richness, not model quality
model_id_length Naming complexity; a weak proxy that may capture versioned or highly descriptive repositories
log_author_model_count Number of models from the same publisher in the latest trending snapshot
log_pipeline_model_count Prevalence of the model's task in the snapshot
log_library_model_count Prevalence of the associated library; missing library is treated as its own group
gated_flag Whether access is automatic/manual gated rather than unrestricted
library_missing Missing library metadata indicator
has_license_tag Whether the tag string contains license metadata
has_arxiv_reference Whether the tags link the model to an arXiv paper

These engineered counts describe the current ecosystem, so conclusions apply to this snapshot, not to the entire Hugging Face Hub. Log transformation handles skew; standardization gives every feature unit variance. Standardization does not make the variables Gaussian and does not remove the special geometry of rare binary indicators.

2.1 Distribution and data-quality findings¶

  • The raw license field is completely missing. This is a collection limitation, not evidence that the repositories lack licenses: 88.5% of the latest rows contain a license: tag.
  • library_name is missing in 13,300 raw rows and 7.9% of the latest snapshot. Missingness is retained explicitly because it may describe a distinct publication pattern.
  • private is constant False, as expected for records returned by a public API, and adds no variance.
  • Download counts, tag counts, and publisher/task/library prevalence have long tails. Log transformation reduces, but does not eliminate, their skewness.
  • The binary gated_flag is rare: 44 of 1,000 models. Once standardized, this rarity gives gated rows a large coordinate value. It can create a cluster that is mathematically coherent but largely driven by one access attribute.
  • The official Hugging Face documentation notes a lower bound around March 2, 2022 for stored creation dates. In this snapshot, 169 rows occur at the two boundary timestamps around that date. Apparent equal ages there are therefore a measurement artifact, not proof that all those repositories were created simultaneously.
  • A high download count or an unusually rich tag list may be legitimate. Boxplot extremes are candidates for investigation, not automatic errors.

2.2 Correlation, tails, and possible artifacts¶

The strongest relationship is between log model age and log days since update ($r=0.822$): older repositories tend also to have older last-update dates. Downloads and likes are positively related but far from interchangeable ($r=0.333$). This leaves substantial variation in machine use that is not mirrored by visible appreciation.

Strong age-recency correlation creates redundancy, so PCA should combine some of their shared variance. Most other absolute correlations are below 0.35. That weak correlation structure is an early warning that a very low-dimensional representation may lose considerable information.

Extreme values can arise from at least four sources: genuinely dominant infrastructure models, new models receiving sudden attention, extensive automatically attached tags, or incomplete/inconsistent metadata. There is no safe basis for deleting them before the anomaly analysis. The pipeline therefore uses monotonic log transforms, keeps all rows, and lets the three detectors disagree.

3. Dimensionality reduction with PCA¶

After standardization, PCA finds orthogonal directions $v_j$ that maximize projected variance. If $S$ is the sample covariance matrix, the first component solves

$$v_1 = \arg\max_{\|v\|=1} v^T S v,$$

and later components solve the same problem subject to orthogonality. The explained-variance ratio for component $j$ is $\lambda_j / \sum_k \lambda_k$.

PCA is global, linear, variance-based, and sensitive to the chosen features and scaling. It does not guarantee preservation of local neighborhoods, cluster density, or anomaly status.

3.1 PCA interpretation¶

  • The first two components retain only 34.7% of standardized variance; three retain 44.5%. A 2D or 3D scatter plot therefore discards most of the information and is primarily a visualization aid.
  • Eight components are needed for at least 80%, ten for 90%, and eleven for 95%. Dimensionality can be reduced modestly, but not compressed to a small plane without substantial loss.
  • PC1 increases with arXiv linkage, likes, age/recency, and tag richness, while decreasing when library metadata is missing. It broadly contrasts documented, established repositories with less documented ones.
  • PC2 is dominated by age and update recency, opposed to author and task prevalence. It separates long-established/less recently updated models from newer models in populous publisher/task groups.
  • PC3 is primarily ecosystem prevalence: common libraries and pipeline types load strongly.
  • PC4 contrasts long or richly tagged identifiers with high downloads, showing that naming/metadata complexity and machine use need not move together.

The original feature set contains one clear redundancy pair (age and update recency), but the slow cumulative-variance curve shows that most information is distributed across different directions. PCA improves visualization and removes correlation, yet it is not a more faithful general representation than the 13-feature space for local density or anomaly detection. It is computationally cheap here, but its components are less directly interpretable than the original variables. Small changes to rare binary features can also rotate later components, so conclusions should emphasize the first components and cumulative variance rather than a single scatter plot.

4. Clustering analysis¶

Three algorithms test different definitions of a cluster.

K-Means¶

K-Means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance:

$$\min_{C_1,\ldots,C_k} \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}\|x_i-\mu_j\|_2^2.$$

It is fast and easy to profile, but assumes centroid-like, roughly spherical groups with similar scale. It requires $k$ and is sensitive to outliers and initialization. I use 30 initializations and a fixed seed.

DBSCAN¶

DBSCAN joins points that have at least min_samples observations within radius $\varepsilon$, expands density-connected regions, and labels unconnected points as noise. It can find non-spherical clusters and does not require $k$, but one global density threshold struggles when density varies or distance concentrates in high dimensions.

Agglomerative clustering¶

Ward agglomeration starts with one cluster per observation and repeatedly merges the pair that causes the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares. It exposes hierarchy and is deterministic for fixed data, but early merges cannot be undone, the cut level must be chosen, and computation/memory scale poorly for very large $n$.

In [9]:
def clustering_metrics(values: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]:
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    keep = labels != -1
    evaluated_labels = labels[keep]
    n_clusters = len(set(evaluated_labels))
    metrics = {
        "clusters": n_clusters,
        "noise_fraction": float((~keep).mean()),
        "silhouette": np.nan,
        "calinski_harabasz": np.nan,
        "davies_bouldin": np.nan,
    }
    if n_clusters >= 2 and keep.sum() > n_clusters:
        metrics.update(
            {
                "silhouette": silhouette_score(values[keep], evaluated_labels),
                "calinski_harabasz": calinski_harabasz_score(values[keep], evaluated_labels),
                "davies_bouldin": davies_bouldin_score(values[keep], evaluated_labels),
            }
        )
    return metrics

def within_global_variance_ratio(values: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    keep = labels != -1
    retained_values = values[keep]
    retained_labels = labels[keep]
    global_variance = retained_values.var(axis=0, ddof=0)
    weighted_within = np.zeros(retained_values.shape[1])
    for label in np.unique(retained_labels):
        group = retained_values[retained_labels == label]
        weighted_within += len(group) * group.var(axis=0, ddof=0)
    weighted_within /= len(retained_values)
    ratios = np.divide(
        weighted_within,
        global_variance,
        out=np.zeros_like(weighted_within),
        where=global_variance > 0,
    )
    return float(ratios.mean())


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
cluster_evaluation = []
for method, labels in cluster_labels.items():
    stability = []
    for trial in range(10):
        perturbed = X_scaled + rng.normal(0, .03, X_scaled.shape)
        if method == "K-Means":
            trial_labels = KMeans(n_clusters=KMEANS_K, n_init=20, random_state=SEED + trial).fit_predict(perturbed)
        elif method == "DBSCAN":
            trial_labels = DBSCAN(eps=DBSCAN_EPS, min_samples=DBSCAN_MIN_SAMPLES).fit_predict(perturbed)
        else:
            trial_labels = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=AGGLOMERATIVE_K, linkage="ward").fit_predict(perturbed)
        stability.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels, trial_labels))
    cluster_evaluation.append(
        {
            "method": method,
            **clustering_metrics(X_scaled, labels),
            "within/global variance": within_global_variance_ratio(X_scaled, labels),
            "mean jitter ARI": np.mean(stability),
            "minimum jitter ARI": np.min(stability),

    )

4.1 Parameter choice and evaluation¶

For K-Means, $k=6$ is a parsimonious point after the main inertia decline. Its silhouette (0.177) is close to the maximum observed at $k=8$ (0.185), while requiring two fewer profiles. Ward clustering is cut at $k=4$, where its silhouette is maximal in the tested range. For DBSCAN, min_samples=15 and the 85th percentile of 15-neighbor distances balance separation with a manageable 4.5% noise rate. Choosing DBSCAN only by its assigned-point silhouette would reward settings that discard many hard observations.

The average within/global variance ratio is appropriate as a compactness diagnostic for K-Means because it matches the geometry the method optimizes. It is not sufficient for model selection: it falls as more clusters are added, ignores between-cluster separation, favors spherical groups, and is especially optimistic for DBSCAN when noise is excluded. Silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin, noise coverage, stability, and interpretability are therefore reported together.

All silhouettes are low (0.177-0.231). The data contain overlapping gradients rather than clean islands. DBSCAN's higher silhouette is calculated only on its assigned points and must be read together with its noise fraction. Small perturbations leave K-Means and DBSCAN mostly stable, but Ward assignments are much less stable, showing that many hierarchical merge decisions are near ties.

4.2 Real-world interpretation¶

K-Means: cluster 0 contains all 44 gated models and has high median likes and tag count; its separation is driven strongly by a rare standardized access feature. Cluster 1 contains established, more downloaded models from publishers with many trending entries. Cluster 2 contains relatively new, lower-engagement models. Cluster 3 is a broad older, modest-engagement group. Cluster 4 is older, rarely updated, and low in likes/tags. Cluster 5 contains newer and recently updated repositories with moderate engagement. These are descriptive personas, not natural species.

DBSCAN: cluster 0 is the large dense core. Cluster 1 captures most, but not all, gated repositories. Clusters 2 and 3 are smaller old/low-engagement and newer/low-engagement regions. The 45 noise points occupy sparse combinations of the features; noise means low density under this parameterization, not incorrect data.

Agglomerative: cluster 0 is a broad mainstream branch, cluster 1 a smaller newer/lower-engagement branch, cluster 2 the gated branch, and cluster 3 an older low-like branch. Its hierarchy exposes broad splits but the perturbation test warns that exact membership is fragile.

Algorithms disagree because they optimize different objects. K-Means partitions every point around centroids, Ward greedily builds a variance hierarchy, and DBSCAN requires density connectivity and may refuse to assign a point. Rare binary indicators, unequal densities, elongated age/recency structure, and weak separation violate the simplest assumptions. In this dataset, cluster profiles are useful summaries, but it would be misleading to claim a single true segmentation.

4.3 Clustering the feature space¶

To cluster features rather than models, I transpose the standardized matrix from $1000\times13$ to $13\times1000$. Euclidean distance between two standardized feature vectors is a monotonic function of their correlation, so nearby feature rows tend to move together across models. Ward clustering is applied to the transpose, and the number of feature groups is selected from $k=2,\ldots,6$ by silhouette.

4.4 What feature clustering adds¶

The best tested cut is four groups, but its silhouette is only 0.135, so the hierarchy is suggestive rather than definitive.

  1. Popularity/documentation/ecosystem footprint: downloads, likes, tag richness, author prevalence, arXiv/license indicators, and gated status form a broad group. These signals tend to co-vary weakly as repositories become more established or documented.
  2. Ecosystem prevalence: task and library prevalence form a tight pair. They measure how common a model's technical context is in the snapshot.
  3. Metadata/naming irregularity: missing library and identifier length form a small group, suggesting that long/specialized names sometimes coincide with incomplete library metadata.
  4. Lifecycle: model age and time since update form the clearest pair, matching their $r=0.822$ correlation and confirming redundancy already visible in PCA.

Clustering samples showed model personas; clustering features exposes dependencies and possible feature hierarchies. This is especially useful in sensor networks, finance, genomics, text representations, and any domain with many correlated measurements, where groups can guide redundancy reduction or domain-specific composite features. Here it suggests that age/recency could be compressed, while most other features should not be removed solely from pairwise correlation.

5. Multi-dimensional anomaly detection¶

An anomaly means an observation that is unusual under a specified representation and method. No ground-truth anomaly label exists, so the goal is comparison and interpretation, not accuracy estimation.

5.1 Classical Z-score¶

For continuous feature $j$,

$$z_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j}{s_j}.$$

A row is classically flagged if any continuous feature has $|z|>3$. This is feature-wise: one extreme coordinate is sufficient. A global alternative such as $\sqrt{\sum_j z_{ij}^2}$ can detect several moderate deviations, but it double-counts correlated variables such as age and update recency; a chi-square interpretation would also be invalid without multivariate Gaussianity and independence. I therefore keep the transparent feature-wise rule as the primary Z-score result. For a fair overlap comparison with methods using 5% contamination, I also rank rows by $\max_j|z_{ij}|$ and take the top 50. Binary indicators are excluded from the classical Z-score because a Gaussian tail interpretation is inappropriate for a rare Bernoulli variable.

The method is transparent and affine-scale invariant, but it assumes mean/standard deviation are meaningful. Skew, heavy tails, correlation, multiple comparisons across dimensions, and anomalies that are unusual only in combinations can all cause failure. As dimension grows, the chance that at least one ordinary coordinate crosses a fixed threshold also grows.

In [15]:
anomaly_budget = int(round(.05 * len(models)))


def top_n_flags(scores: np.ndarray, n: int = anomaly_budget) -> np.ndarray:
    scores = np.asarray(scores)
    flags = np.zeros(len(scores), dtype=bool)
    flags[np.argpartition(scores, -n)[-n:]] = True
    return flags

5.2 Isolation Forest¶

Isolation Forest repeatedly selects a random feature and a random split between that feature's observed minimum and maximum. Unusual observations tend to be isolated after fewer splits. If $h(x)$ is path length and $c(\psi)$ is the expected unsuccessful search length for subsample size $\psi$, the original anomaly score is

$$s(x,\psi)=2^{-E[h(x)]/c(\psi)}.$$

High original scores mean short paths and greater abnormality; values near 0.5 are less decisive. Scikit-learn exposes lower score_samples values for more abnormal rows, so I negate them: larger reported values are more anomalous and smaller values are more typical.

contamination=0.05 does not discover that 5% of reality is abnormal; it sets the decision threshold so exactly 5% of this sample is flagged. The ensemble handles nonlinear interactions and high-dimensional data better than a univariate rule, but results depend on the included features, randomness, contamination, and whether anomalies can be isolated by axis-aligned cuts.

In [16]:
start = perf_counter()
isolation_forest = IsolationForest(
    n_estimators=400,
    contamination=.05,
    random_state=SEED,
    n_jobs=-1,
)
isolation_labels = isolation_forest.fit_predict(X_scaled)
isolation_scores = -isolation_forest.score_samples(X_scaled)
isolation_flags = isolation_labels == -1
runtime_seconds["Isolation Forest"] = perf_counter() - start

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(projection["PC1"], projection["PC2"], c="#B8B8B8", s=20, alpha=.45, label="Not flagged")
ax.scatter(projection.loc[isolation_flags, "PC1"], projection.loc[isolation_flags, "PC2"], c="#F58518", s=42, label="Isolation Forest")

5.3 Local Outlier Factor (LOF)¶

LOF compares a point's local reachability density with those of its neighbors. In simplified form,

$$LOF_k(x)=\frac{1}{|N_k(x)|}\sum_{o\in N_k(x)}\frac{lrd_k(o)}{lrd_k(x)}.$$

Values near 1 indicate density similar to neighboring points; values above 1 indicate a sparser local neighborhood. LOF can identify a local anomaly hidden inside a globally broad distribution, but Euclidean neighborhoods become unstable when dimensions increase or scales are unequal. Small $k$ reacts to microstructure and noise; large $k$ becomes more global and can wash out small groups. I use $k=35$ as an intermediate neighborhood and explicitly compare alternatives.

In [17]:
lof_sensitivity_rows = []
lof_outputs = {}
for neighbors in [10, 20, 35, 50, 75, 100]:
    start = perf_counter()
    detector = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=neighbors, contamination=.05)
    labels = detector.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    elapsed = perf_counter() - start
    lof_outputs[neighbors] = {
        "flags": labels == -1,
        "scores": -detector.negative_outlier_factor_,
        "runtime": elapsed,
    }

LOF_K = 35
lof_flags = lof_outputs[LOF_K]["flags"]
lof_scores = lof_outputs[LOF_K]["scores"]
runtime_seconds["LOF"] = lof_outputs[LOF_K]["runtime"]
for neighbors, result in lof_outputs.items():
    comparison = result["flags"]
    lof_sensitivity_rows.append(
        {
            "neighbors": neighbors,
            "flagged": int(comparison.sum()),
            "Jaccard vs k=35": (comparison & lof_flags).sum() / (comparison | lof_flags).sum(),
            "runtime_seconds": result["runtime"],
        }
    )
lof_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(lof_sensitivity_rows)
display(lof_sensitivity)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))

The classical Z-score threshold produces its own data-dependent count. For direct method overlap, all three rankings are also compared at a common 5% review budget (50 models). This separates the question "what does the textbook threshold flag?" from "which 50 cases would each method prioritize?"

def jaccard_score_flags(left: np.ndarray, right: np.ndarray) -> float:
    left = np.asarray(left, dtype=bool)
    right = np.asarray(right, dtype=bool)
    return float((left & right).sum() / (left | right).sum())


# Scaling sensitivity: same 13 transformed features, before and after StandardScaler.
X_unscaled = X.to_numpy(float)
z_unscaled_flags = top_n_flags(np.abs(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X[continuous_features])).max(axis=1))
if_unscaled_model = IsolationForest(n_estimators=400, contamination="auto", random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_unscaled)
if_unscaled_flags = top_n_flags(-if_unscaled_model.score_samples(X_unscaled))
lof_unscaled_model = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=LOF_K).fit(X_unscaled)
lof_unscaled_flags = top_n_flags(-lof_unscaled_model.negative_outlier_factor_)

# Dimensionality sensitivity: refit in the PCA space retaining at least 90% variance.
pca90_components = components_needed[.90]
X_pca90 = pca_scores[:, :pca90_components]
z_pca90_flags = top_n_flags(np.abs(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_pca90)).max(axis=1))
if_pca90_model = IsolationForest(n_estimators=400, contamination="auto", random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_pca90)
if_pca90_flags = top_n_flags(-if_pca90_model.score_samples(X_pca90))
lof_pca90_model = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=LOF_K).fit(X_pca90)
lof_pca90_flags = top_n_flags(-lof_pca90_model.negative_outlier_factor_)

# Robustness to small measurement noise: mean Jaccard over five 3% Gaussian perturbations.
noise_rows = []
for method, baseline in [
    ("Z-score", z_equal_budget_flags),
    ("Isolation Forest", isolation_flags),
    ("LOF", lof_flags),
]:
    agreements = []
    for trial in range(5):
        jittered = X_scaled + np.random.default_rng(SEED + trial).normal(0, .03, X_scaled.shape)
        if method == "Z-score":
            alternative = top_n_flags(np.abs(jittered[:, : len(continuous_features)]).max(axis=1))
        elif method == "Isolation Forest":
            fitted = IsolationForest(n_estimators=400, contamination="auto", random_state=SEED + trial, n_jobs=-1).fit(jittered)
            alternative = top_n_flags(-fitted.score_samples(jittered))
        else:
            fitted = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=LOF_K).fit(jittered)
            alternative = top_n_flags(-fitted.negative_outlier_factor_)
        agreements.append(jaccard_score_flags(baseline, alternative))
    noise_rows.append({"method": method, "mean_jaccard": np.mean(agreements), "minimum_jaccard": np.min(agreements)})

sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"method": "Z-score", "scaling_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(z_equal_budget_flags, z_unscaled_flags), "PCA90_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(z_equal_budget_flags, z_pca90_flags)},
        {"method": "Isolation Forest", "scaling_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(isolation_flags, if_unscaled_flags), "PCA90_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(isolation_flags, if_pca90_flags)},
        {"method": "LOF", "scaling_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(lof_flags, lof_unscaled_flags), "PCA90_jaccard": jaccard_score_flags(lof_flags, lof_pca90_flags)},
    ]
).merge(pd.DataFrame(noise_rows), on="method")
sensitivity["runtime_seconds"] = sensitivity["method"].map(runtime_seconds)
display(sensitivity)

6.1 Agreement and method-specific anomalies¶

At the common 5% budget, only seven models are selected by all three methods, and 115 are selected by at least one. Pairwise Jaccard agreement is low: 0.075 for Z-score/Isolation Forest, 0.266 for Z-score/LOF, and 0.163 for Isolation Forest/LOF. The detectors are not interchangeable.

  • Z-score prioritizes a single extreme continuous coordinate, such as very high downloads or tag count.
  • Isolation Forest finds combinations that require unusually short random partition paths, even when no coordinate exceeds three standard deviations.
  • LOF finds points whose density is low relative to their particular neighborhood. Its selected set changes sharply with $k$, confirming strong neighborhood sensitivity.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice is a useful ambiguous example. All three methods flag it, largely because its tag count is 657 while its downloads and age are not comparably extreme. That can be a legitimate, heavily annotated speech repository rather than a data error. sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is another legitimate but unusual case: extremely high infrastructure use makes it globally exceptional even though nothing is inherently wrong with the repository.

6.2 Scaling, dimensionality, runtime, and noise¶

The sensitivity table reports empirical Jaccard overlap rather than relying only on theory. Z-score is affine-scale invariant because it standardizes internally. Isolation Forest is nearly invariant to independent positive rescaling of each feature because axis-aligned split order is preserved. LOF is strongly scale-sensitive because raw large-range coordinates dominate Euclidean neighborhoods.

Using only the PCA components needed for 90% variance changes all three review lists. Variance preservation is not anomaly preservation: low-variance directions can contain rare behavior. This is why the anomaly plots in 2D may hide points detected in 13 dimensions or make projected edge points look suspicious when their full-space neighborhood is ordinary.

On 1,000 rows, all runtimes are small. The theoretical difference matters at scale: Z-score is $O(nd)$; Isolation Forest is approximately $O(t\,\psi\log\psi)$ for $t$ trees and subsample size $\psi$; exact LOF neighbor search can approach $O(n^2d)$ when tree-based neighbor search deteriorates in high dimensions. Under small Gaussian perturbations, Z-score and LOF rankings are stable here, while Isolation Forest varies more because both the data and randomized partitions change.

6.3 Interpretability and robustness¶

Z-score is easiest to explain and names the extreme feature, but Gaussian tail language is unreliable for the skewed distributions. Isolation Forest captures interactions and scales well, but its score is less tied to one business reason. LOF has an intuitive local-density interpretation, but a result is inseparable from its neighborhood definition. No method is robust to arbitrary noise, missing variables, or a badly chosen representation.

6.4 False positives and false negatives without labels¶

There is no confirmed normal/anomalous label, so a numeric confusion matrix would be invented. In this context, a false positive would send a legitimate repository for unnecessary review; repeated false alarms would waste analyst time and cause alert fatigue. A false negative would miss corrupted metadata, manipulation, a sudden popularity event, or another genuinely important change. Which error is worse depends on the intended use. A low-cost metadata audit may favor recall; suspending model access would require much higher precision and human verification.

7. Critical analysis and reflection¶

Why anomaly detection is ill-defined¶

Anomaly detection has no universal target. Rare, surprising, harmful, erroneous, and novel are different concepts. A blockbuster model, a gated model, and a malformed row can all be statistically unusual for different reasons. Contamination and thresholds encode operational choices, not natural laws. Without reviewed examples, agreement supports prioritization but does not prove correctness.

Curse of dimensionality¶

As dimension grows, data occupy an exponentially larger space. Samples become sparse, local neighborhoods contain fewer genuinely comparable points, and nearest and farthest distances can become similar relative to their scale. This concentration weakens the meaning of Euclidean distance for LOF and DBSCAN. Irrelevant features also add noise to every distance. Standardization fixes units, not sparsity or relevance.

Noise versus a genuine anomaly¶

Noise is an unreliable measurement or random fluctuation; a genuine anomaly is a valid observation that matters for the question. k2-fsa/OmniVoice may be genuine because an unusually large tag list can reflect broad compatibility or automated metadata. A broken parser that duplicated tags would instead be noise. The numbers alone cannot decide; the repository card and collection pipeline would need verification.

Risks of Gaussian assumptions¶

Downloads and tag counts retain positive skew and excess kurtosis after logs, while the binary fields are not Gaussian at all. A fixed Z threshold may over-flag legitimate heavy-tail observations, and mean/standard deviation can themselves be distorted by extremes. Conversely, a point that is moderate in every marginal feature but has an impossible combination can be missed. Correlation also means feature-wise tests are not independent.

Why PCA pictures can mislead¶

The 2D plane retains only 34.7% of standardized variance. Distant full-space points can overlap after projection, and apparently separated points can differ mainly along two high-variance directions while being ordinary in the remaining dimensions. PCA preserves global variance, not local density, cluster membership, or anomaly scores. Every PCA anomaly/cluster plot in this notebook is therefore a display of full-space decisions, not the space used to make those decisions.

Methodological limitations¶

  • The latest snapshot removes repeated-row dependence but discards growth trajectories.
  • The source includes trending models, so the sample is selected toward visibility and is not representative of the full Hub.
  • Download counts are rolling 30-day activity, not unique users or value created.
  • Likes, tags, and model cards are influenced by publisher behavior and community norms.
  • Feature engineering embeds choices about what counts as ecosystem prominence or metadata richness.
  • Rare binary features can dominate standardized distances.
  • The analysis validates internal geometry and stability, not external truth.

A stronger follow-up would combine time-series growth features, authoritative model-card checks for flagged rows, mixed-type distances, robust covariance baselines, and expert-reviewed anomaly labels.

Ethical considerations¶

False alarms: If every unusual model triggers escalation, reviewers learn to ignore the system. High-impact actions should never be based on an unsupervised score alone.

Surveillance: Anomaly detection can surface abuse or compromised accounts, but broad behavioral monitoring can invade privacy and chill legitimate experimentation. Purpose limitation, minimum data collection, access controls, and appeal mechanisms are essential.

Medicine: A false positive can cause anxiety, unnecessary tests, and cost; a false negative can delay treatment. Clinical systems require validated labels, subgroup performance checks, and clinician oversight. This notebook's exploratory workflow would not be sufficient.

Cybersecurity: Missing a real attack can expose systems and data, while flagging legitimate activity can block work and overwhelm responders. Thresholds should reflect asset criticality, and alerts need contextual evidence.

Bias and fairness: Underrepresented publishers, languages, tasks, or licensing practices may look anomalous simply because the dataset contains fewer of them. Labeling a repository, person, or behavior as "abnormal" can stigmatize difference and amplify historical sampling bias. Scores should be framed as review priorities, documented, audited across subgroups, and contestable.

    signature_rows.append(pd.Series(X_scaled[flags].mean(axis=0), index=feature_columns, name=method))
signature = pd.DataFrame(signature_rows)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(signature.rename(columns=feature_labels), cmap="vlag", center=0, annot=True, fmt=".1f", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Average standardized feature signature of each detector's top 5%")
ax.set_xlabel("")
fig.tight_layout()
save_figure("18_anomaly_signature_heatmap.png")
plt.show()

9. Conclusions¶

  1. The latest-snapshot data do not contain strongly separated natural clusters. Six K-Means personas, four Ward branches, and four DBSCAN density regions summarize different aspects of a mostly continuous, overlapping space.
  2. Age and update recency are genuinely redundant, but PCA still needs ten components to retain 90% of the 13-feature variance. Two-dimensional views are lossy.
  3. Feature clustering confirms a lifecycle pair and an ecosystem-prevalence pair, while most other relationships are weak.
  4. The classical Z-score flags 70 rows at $|z|>3$. At a matched 5% budget, the three anomaly methods agree on only seven models, demonstrating that "anomaly" depends on global extremes, random isolation, or local density.
  5. The most defensible output is a prioritized review list with method reasons, not a declaration that 50 models are bad. Real-world verification is required before any action.
